extracted.intended_audience: telephone companies, interveners, counsel, and other parties participating in CRTC telecommunications filings and hearings
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and evidentiary rules and recommended practices for making applications to, intervening in, and participating in CRTC telecommunications hearings (including notice, interrogatories, pre-hearing steps, hearing conduct, and post‑filing processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part application filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must now be in two parts, the first containing the material formerly filed under the CTC's practice accompanied by a table showing the present and proposed rates, and the second part consisting of supporting memoranda containing all the evidence and exhibits intended to be introduced at the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memoranda must also describe in detail the progress and current status of any outstanding matters raised in the most recent decision of the Commission respecting general rates. The attempt is to permit interveners to know at the outset the entire case of the applicant so they can assess whether to intervene and prepare interrogatories; it also saves time at the hearing because evidence-in-chief can be tabled and updated by witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive public notice is required: a simplified form of notice spelling out the changes applied for and the reasons must be published in all newspapers of general circulation specified by the Commission; applicants must also mail to each telephone subscriber a notice similar to that published in the newspapers; copies of the application and the Commission's directions on procedure must be placed in each of the company's business offices for public inspection; registered 'interested parties' must be served with all material filed by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to ensure wide public awareness and to provide opportunities for comment or intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices set out three methods of intervention: (1) send a letter of comment to the Commission, (2) make a submission at a regional hearing in addition to or in lieu of sending a letter of comment, and (3) fully participate in the central hearing by filing a 'notice of intention to participate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This accommodates various classes of interested persons according to the extent of their desired involvement; extent of participation varies inversely with time/resources required by each form of intervention (example: thousands of written comments vs dozens participating in central hearing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatory entitlement and response obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone who has filed a notice of intention to participate may address interrogatories to the applicant. Interrogatories are questions put in writing to the applicant on any aspect of the application. Under the Rules, the applicant is required to respond to all interrogatories thus furnished to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant is unable or unwilling to furnish a full and adequate response because the information sought is not relevant, unavailable, or confidential, the Rules direct that full reasons supporting these grounds must be supplied. Interrogatories are traditionally numerous and wide-ranging (e.g., nearly one thousand in the Bell Canada case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-hearing conference and consolidated interrogatory list
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-hearing conference is used to deal with interrogatories for which answers have not been supplied to the satisfaction of interveners and other preliminary points of procedure. Interrogatories still in issue are normally disposed of by the Commission preparing a consolidated list of interrogatories which call for the information it considers the applicant should supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-hearing conference is usually chaired by a Commissioner who will sit at the central hearing; once the Commission is satisfied it has received the information it requires, the matter is ready for hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional hearing format and notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional hearings are conducted along the lines of a public meeting: any person or association affected may read or expand upon a letter of comment or make other submissions. Representatives of the regulated company may ask questions of clarification but not cross-examine. A person wishing to appear must notify the Commission orally or in writing at least twenty-four hours before the commencement of the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional hearings provide a mechanism for subscribers to appear and air views without the time and expense of central hearing participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central hearing sequence and witness procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: At the central hearing, witnesses for the applicant appear first, state their qualifications, and may update their memorandum of evidence previously filed. Cross-examination is conducted by interveners in a pre-determined order; the CRTC's counsel cross-examines after interveners and usually takes the last spot. Following the applicant's evidence, interveners call witnesses; the applicant may call rebuttal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memoranda of evidence to be presented by witnesses must be filed in writing with the Commission at least forty-eight hours in advance of the appearance of the witnesses and copies provided to all other parties. This sequencing and deadline aim to structure testimony and cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concluding arguments (oral or written) and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission may require that concluding arguments be made orally or in writing; the normal practice is oral argument, but in complex cases the Commission has adjourned proceedings after all evidence and required written arguments to be filed according to prescribed deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written argument shortens sitting time and allows more comprehensive, fully developed arguments, assisting the Commission in making and writing its decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of informality measures in hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has tried to create an atmosphere of informality by using meeting rooms instead of court rooms, allowing witnesses and counsel to remain seated, and permitting witnesses to sit in panels while giving evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although procedures remain more formal than broadcasting hearings due to technical complexity and voluminous evidence, these measures aim to reduce formality's burdens while retaining necessary discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission articulation of relevant issues prior to hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission could and should take a more active role in refining the issues and indicating to the parties in advance of the hearing the matters it considers relevant to its decision on the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike judges, Commissioners may identify public interest principles and how they should be applied; after all written material is filed, the Commission should be at liberty to articulate in detail matters on which it wishes further information or argument. Settling issues beforehand would help restrain random or duplicative cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set list of issues after pre-hearing conference
rubrics_metrics.description: At a reasonable time before the central hearing begins the Commission should settle the issues on which the hearing should proceed. This could be done after a pre-hearing conference at which the parties are provided a preliminary list of issues drawn up by the Commission and given an opportunity to comment and suggest changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence of such a list would put a smaller framework around the hearing and help to restrain random cross-examination; helps eliminate repetitive issues that have been previously decided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervener statement of position and earlier evidence filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Interveners should be required to file a statement of their positions and memoranda of the evidence of their witnesses earlier than the current forty-eight hour rule—i.e., prior to the commencement of the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier disclosure is fairer to applicants and gives them reasonable opportunity to prepare cross-examination; interveners can still supplement evidence (file outline of supplementary evidence under current 48-hour rule). Recommendation: require filing of statement of position prior to hearing commencement, setting out support, opposition, or requested modifications and reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit or curb neutral interveners' broad cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing interveners (e.g., provincial governments, Director of Investigation and Research) to take neutral positions throughout the hearing has resulted in very broad and lengthy cross-examination without focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interveners should be able to take a preliminary stance based on available information; preliminary positions would not prevent modification later. Reducing neutral, unfocused questioning would reduce delays and help parties prepare witnesses and rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and vetting of interrogatories by the Commission
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrogatories should be channelled through the Commission (which would act as a control centre) to sort out inappropriate, irrelevant and repetitive questions, using a single consecutive numbering scheme and a vetting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended procedure: (a) each intervener prepares a complete list of questions after filing of evidence; (b) list is served on all parties including the Commission; (c) a conference chaired by a senior official is held to address relevance, duplication, confidentiality; (d) Commission decides which questions must be answered, publishes a list and responses are obtained; (e) same procedure for supplementary interrogatories. This would avoid duplication, confusion, and excessive burden on applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize interrogatories for rate hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRTC is attempting to standardize interrogatories for rate hearings to prevent duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization will help prevent repetitive questions and make organizing and digesting answers more manageable; part of broader recommendation that Commission vet interrogatories centrally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage application process for capital issues
rubrics_metrics.description: For capital stock issues (Bell Canada and British Columbia Telephone Company), the Commission has introduced a two-stage application process: first stage—file a detailed application setting out the capital amount sought and type of equity issue, with evidence on need for capital, financing choice, and debt-equity ratio; copies forwarded to interveners who can comment and, absent serious problems, approved 'in principle' without public hearing; second stage—on the day the company determines actual price and final terms, this information is provided to the Commission and interested interveners; if terms do not substantially depart from those approved in principle, the Commission gives approval on the same day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balances market realities with desire for public involvement and allows timely approvals while preserving oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tariff filing supporting documentation and economic evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tariff Filing Guidelines spell out kinds of supporting information required for various categories of tariff revisions. In most cases, an economic evaluation must accompany the filing to show that the service has been priced so as not to be a burden on other services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A special standing committee reviews tariff applications (quorum of at least two Commissioners), staff analysts prepare formal agendas and recommendations; though initially more time-consuming, decisions are now being announced within 30 days for the majority of routine filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscriber complaint procedure and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints are made by delivering a letter to the Commission setting out the facts and requesting specific relief. If the Commission believes the complaint should be investigated it forwards a copy or summary to the regulated company requesting comment, and the company must reply within twenty days or such other period as the Commission may determine. If neither party requests oral hearing, the Commission may deal with the matter on the basis of written documentation or issue directions for an oral hearing. Emergency relief may be sought orally and the Commission may issue interim ex-parte orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part VI codifies complaint procedures and shows the Commission treats subscriber complaints with detailed attention; timelines (20 days for company reply) and ability to handle emergency ex‑parte relief are key practical rules.
